entries.short: In meme slang: opposite of “alpha” — portrayed as passive or less dominant (often rude/joke).
entries.explain: Internet “beta” is usually an insult or ironic label in alpha/sigma meme talk — not the software “beta test” meaning, and not a clinical term. Judgment-free tip: people throw it around loosely; it’s more meme than science.
entries.origin: Same pop hierarchy memes as alpha; gaming/internet culture.

entries.short: In TikTok/internet slang: top-dog / “best” / dominant vibe — not the Greek letter.
entries.explain: Online, calling someone (or yourself) “alpha” usually means confident, high-status, in charge, or “that girl/guy is the best.” It’s meme language from manosphere/self-help crossover into general TikTok. Tone ranges from serious flex to ironic joke. Separately, alpha is also the first Greek letter and a software “early version” word — but if you saw it on TikTok, they almost certainly mean the slang status vibe.
entries.origin: Pop-psych “alpha/beta” animal hierarchy metaphors → internet debate culture → TikTok shorthand for elite/dominant energy.

entries.short: YouTube/TikTok horror-comedy series by DaFuq!?Boom! with heads in toilets; kids also chant “skibidi” as brainrot noise.
entries.explain: Skibidi Toilet is a surreal animated series by DaFuq!?Boom! (Alexey Gerasimov): singing human heads in toilets fight camera-headed people (Cameramen) and other hardware-headed factions. On playgrounds and the FYP, “skibidi” is often just a nonsense chant — participation, not a secret code. Asking what it means is normal; the joke is how little dictionary sense it has.
entries.origin: YouTube series by DaFuq!?Boom!, 2023–; exploded on TikTok and in Gen Alpha schoolyard/brainrot culture.

entries.short: Catch-all punchline for anything chaotic, cursed, or strangely specific — rarely about the actual state.
entries.explain: Gen Alpha / TikTok treats Ohio as the capital of weird internet energy. “Only in Ohio” captions cursed clips; “you’re Ohio” just means you’re being weird. Judgment-free: it’s a meme geography, not a travel review.
entries.origin: TikTok / Gen Alpha brainrot meme.

entries.short: A loud reaction to someone’s body, especially hips/backside — like an exaggerated “goddamn.”
entries.explain: Used as a hype shout, caption, or joke. It can feel objectifying depending on tone; Trendy just explains the slang, not the stare. Not a rating system.
entries.origin: Stream/TikTok slang (from ‘goddamn’); brainrot vocabulary.

entries.short: Playfully taking a bite of someone else’s food — a ‘tax’ named after streamer Fanum.
entries.explain: Friends joke that a bite of your snack is owed as Fanum tax. It’s a bit from AMP / Kai Cenat’s circle, not a real fee. Asking is allowed; nobody expects you to already know the streamer lore.
entries.origin: Streamer Fanum (AMP); TikTok/YouTube clips.

entries.short: Tongue-posture trend people claim will change a jawline.
entries.explain: Looksmaxxing lore: rest your tongue on the roof of your mouth. Some treat it as a glow-up hack; others treat it as a joke pose. Not medical advice — just internet face-training slang.
entries.origin: Orthotropics discourse → TikTok looksmaxxing explainers.

entries.short: Internet slang for a lone-wolf “cool outsider” archetype (cousin of “alpha” memes).
entries.explain: On TikTok, “sigma” is a personality meme: independent, quiet-confident, not needing the crowd. Often half-joke. Related to alpha/beta meme vocabulary.
entries.origin: Online personality-type memes adjacent to alpha discourse; exploded on TikTok/Reels.

entries.short: Looking so much more attractive that you ‘mog’ someone else’s looks by comparison.
entries.explain: Looksmaxxing slang for winning a looks comparison (face, height, vibe). Can be a joke ranking or a mean dunk. Explaining the word isn’t endorsing the hierarchy.
entries.origin: Looksmaxxing forums → TikTok/brainrot speech.

entries.short: Trying to optimize appearance with routines, tips, and sometimes extreme advice.
entries.explain: Covers everything from skincare and gym to controversial ‘maxxing’ discourse. Trendy explains the term people are seeing, not an ideology. Glow-up curiosity is allowed.
entries.origin: Forum slang that hit TikTok explainers.

entries.short: Hovering at the edge of a payoff without finishing — a joke about delay and tension.
entries.explain: People say they’re edging when they stretch a wait (a reveal, a win, or an innuendo) without going over. In casual TikTok use it’s usually a bit, not a how-to. Keep it PG: the slang is about delay, not instructions.
entries.origin: Older slang recycled as a TikTok/stream joke.

entries.short: A snap read of whether the energy is good, off, or a little dangerous.
entries.explain: Can be a joke (‘vibe check ✨’) or a real ‘are you OK / is this room safe’ scan. Passing a vibe check just means the energy landed.
entries.origin: 2010s internet → still common on TikTok and in group chats.

entries.short: Content so absurd or repetitive it feels like it rewires your brain — often said with affection.
entries.explain: A self-aware label for hyper-online meme loops (skibidi, 67, Ohio, etc.). Calling something brainrot can mean ‘this is unserious and I love it’ more than an insult. Nobody is behind for not speaking fluent brainrot yet.
entries.origin: Internet-culture label; TikTok FYP is the main greenhouse.

entries.short: Invisible cool-points — you gain or lose aura based on how a moment lands.
entries.explain: Aura farming is doing something on purpose to look effortlessly cool. Losing aura is secondhand cringe. Playful social scoring, not mysticism.
entries.origin: Gaming/stream slang → TikTok.

entries.short: Over-the-top praise or riding for someone — complimenting so hard it gets embarrassing.
entries.explain: If you’re glazing, you’re hyping a person (or yourself) past the point of chill. Can be teasing (‘stop glazing’) or a roast. Not a baking tutorial.
entries.origin: AAVE/rap slang → TikTok captions and live chat.

entries.short: Doomed, in trouble, or exhausted — the situation is already over.
entries.explain: ‘You’re cooked’ means you messed up or you’re about to. Opposite energy of ‘let him cook’ (let them cook = let them cook / they’re on a roll). Tone is usually playful panic.
entries.origin: Internet slang; sports and school chats use it constantly.

entries.short: Talking a lot — rambling, oversharing, or excitedly going on.
entries.explain: A yapper is someone who will not stop talking. Can be affectionate (‘let her yap’) or a ‘please get to the point.’ Very online, very harmless.
entries.origin: Older slang revived as TikTok/stream chat vocabulary.

entries.short: Losing it — overreacting, spiraling, or going off after holding it in.
entries.explain: A crash out is a blow-up (anger, tears, reckless choices). People also joke ‘don’t crash out’ as a vibe-check. Describes the moment; doesn’t diagnose anyone.
entries.origin: AAVE → TikTok/Twitter mainstream.

entries.short: Gen Alpha / TikTok brainrot catchphrase — yelled for the bit, not a literal code.
entries.explain: Kids shout ‘six seven’ with a hand gesture because the sound/meme is the joke. There isn’t a hidden dictionary meaning; participating in the noise is the point. You’re not late for asking.
entries.origin: TikTok sounds (notably Skrilla’s “Doot Doot (6 7)”) and hallway copycat energy.

entries.short: Really good — especially food, but also fits, music, or a moment.
entries.explain: ‘This is bussin’ ≈ this slaps / this is delicious. Casual praise; not a technical review.
entries.origin: AAVE → wider Gen Z/TikTok use.

entries.short: Fully focused — no distractions, main-character concentration.
entries.explain: Sports, school, and streamers say lock in before a grind session. Opposite of crashing out or yapping through the assignment.
entries.origin: Sports/gaming talk → TikTok study/grind culture.

entries.short: Let them cook — don’t interrupt, they’re onto something.
entries.explain: A hype green light: give the person room to finish the idea, play, or rant. Opposite of shutting someone down mid-yap. Not about actual cooking unless the video is.
entries.origin: Sports/internet hype phrase; everywhere on TikTok.

entries.short: Laughing out loud (or a softer chuckle online).
entries.explain: Originally meant actual laughing. Now it's often just a softener — 'lol ok' can mean acknowledgment, awkwardness, or mild amusement. LMAO / LMFAO are louder variants. Nobody is judging you for using it; almost everyone does.
entries.origin: Early internet / SMS culture, 1980s–90s Usenet and chat rooms.

entries.explain: A wink that the joke or reference is for people already in on it. Used in captions when explaining would kill the vibe. Related energy: 'you had to be there.'
entries.origin: Social captions and stan Twitter; now everywhere.

entries.explain: Having rizz means you can charm someone. Unspoken rizz is magnetism without trying. Rizzless means the opposite. It's playful slang, not a clinical diagnosis of your dating life.
entries.origin: Streamers / Gen Z slang (popularized by Kai Cenat); Oxford Word of the Year 2023.

entries.short: The problem is your skill, not the game (or situation).
entries.explain: A gaming roast that migrated to general internet use. Can be affectionate teasing ('skill issue fr') or a dunk. Tone depends on the friend group.
entries.origin: Competitive gaming chats; now general meme slang.

entries.short: Non-player character — acting scripted or background.
entries.explain: From games: characters that follow fixed paths and repeat lines. Calling someone NPC energy suggests they're predictable or not 'main character.' Can be self-deprecating or mean — context matters.
entries.origin: Gaming → meme culture / TikTok.

entries.short: Good game — polite match ending (EZ = toxic gloat).
entries.explain: GG is sportsmanship after a match. GG EZ (easy) is a taunt. Many communities frown on EZ spam. Alone, GG still means 'respect, match over.'
entries.origin: Competitive gaming etiquette.

entries.short: Log off and go outside / reconnect with reality.
entries.explain: Tells someone they're too online. Can be caring ('maybe touch grass') or a roast. Pair often with 'chronically online.'
entries.origin: Meme and gaming spaces → mainstream.

entries.explain: Softened 'delusional,' especially about crushes, fame fantasies, or shipping. 'Delulu is the solulu' jokes that believing your fantasy is a coping strategy. Usually affectionate chaos, not a medical claim.
entries.origin: K-pop / stan spaces → TikTok mainstream.

entries.explain: FOMO is anxiety that others are having more fun. JOMO is the flip: pleasure in missing the party on purpose. Both show up in wellness and social media discourse.
entries.origin: Marketing / social media vocabulary (2000s–2010s).

entries.explain: Praise for looks, performance, or confidence. 'You slayed' ≈ you crushed it. Roots in ballroom / drag culture; mainstreamed via social media.
entries.origin: Ballroom and LGBTQ+ vernacular → viral TikTok / Twitter.

entries.short: Cap = lie; no cap = not lying / for real.
entries.explain: If someone is capping, they're exaggerating or lying. 'No cap' means you're being honest. Common in captions and voice notes.
entries.origin: AAVE → wider Gen Z slang.

entries.explain: Like saying 'alright' or 'sounds good.' Context can also mean 'challenge accepted.' Short, casual, friendly.
entries.origin: AAVE → mainstream youth slang.

entries.short: Suspicious — popularized hard by Among Us.
entries.explain: Something or someone feels off. Among Us made it ubiquitous; still used for anything shady or questionable.
entries.origin: Older slang; exploded with Among Us (2020).

entries.short: Unapologetically authentic (or agreeing with a take).
entries.explain: Originally from rapper Lil B's positivity; later picked up in meme politics. In casual use it often just means 'I respect that take' or 'standing on business.' Be aware it can carry edgier connotations in some corners.
entries.origin: Lil B → 4chan / meme culture → general internet.

entries.explain: A soft roast. Calling something mid means it's average or disappointing — not the worst, just not it.
entries.origin: Gen Z slang / gaming adjacent.

entries.short: Performed or looked so good there's nothing left to critique.
entries.explain: High praise, often about fashion, makeup, or a performance. 'Left no crumbs' doubles down: flawless.
entries.origin: Black Twitter / LGBTQ+ slang → TikTok.

entries.explain: BRB = be right back; AFK = away from keyboard; TTYL = talk to you later; IMO/IMHO = in my (humble) opinion; TBH = to be honest; IDK = I don't know; SMH = shaking my head; NVM = never mind; OMG / WTF = surprise / frustration. Old-school but still everywhere.
entries.origin: Early chat rooms, SMS, and forums.

entries.short: A snack plate that counts as dinner — vibes over rules.
entries.explain: Assembling random fridge finds into a meal without guilt. Celebrates low-effort eating; not gendered in practice despite the name.
entries.origin: TikTok trend / confession format.

entries.short: Living like the protagonist of your own story.
entries.explain: Confidence aesthetic: walking with purpose, romanticizing your day. Opposite vibe of NPC energy. Usually playful self-mythologizing.
entries.origin: TikTok / self-help adjacent meme culture.

entries.short: When replies vastly outnumber likes — usually a dunk.
entries.explain: On Twitter/X, getting ratioed means the crowd disagreed hard. People reply 'ratio' to try to make it happen. A social-proof roast.
entries.origin: Twitter culture.
